content: A febrile seizure, also referred to as a fever fit or febrile convulsion, is a generalized seizure that occurs due to an elevated body temperature. These seizures are most commonly observed in children under the age of three and are not typically diagnosed in children younger than six months or older than six years. In many cases, the seizure itself may be the first indication of a fever. It is hypothesized that the rapid rise in body temperature, rather than the absolute temperature reached, is the primary trigger for the seizure. Febrile seizures are classified into two main categories: 1. Simple Febrile Seizures: These seizures last less than 15 minutes. They are generalized, meaning they affect the entire body. They do not recur during the same febrile illness. 2. Complex Febrile Seizures: These seizures may have focal features, affecting only part of the body. They last longer than 15 minutes. They may recur within 24 hours during the same febrile illness. Febrile seizures occur at the intersection of a low seizure threshold (which is influenced by genetic and age-related factors) and a triggering event, such as fever. Some children are genetically predisposed to have a lower seizure threshold, making them more susceptible to seizures under certain conditions. While the genetic causes of febrile seizures are still under investigation, some mutations that lead to neuronal hyperexcitability have already been identified. The diagnosis of febrile seizures is made by excluding more serious causes of seizures, such as meningitis or encephalitis. A physician's evaluation is essential, and in many cases, the child may be admitted to the hospital for overnight observation and/or diagnostic tests. If the child returns to a normal state of health shortly after the seizure, an infection of the nervous system is considered unlikely. Even when a febrile seizure is diagnosed, physicians will aim to identify and treat the underlying cause of the fever. It is important to distinguish between simple and complex febrile seizures. Simple febrile seizures, which are the most common type, are less concerning. They typically involve the entire body, last less than 15 minutes, and do not recur within 24 hours. Complex febrile seizures, on the other hand, are characterized by longer duration, recurrence, or focal features. Simple febrile seizures are generally reassuring because they do not cause permanent brain injury, are unlikely to recur frequently, and do not significantly increase the risk of developing epilepsy in adulthood (the risk is less than 3-5%, similar to the general population). Children who are at higher risk of developing afebrile epileptic seizures in the future often exhibit the following characteristics: A family history of afebrile seizures in first-degree relatives (such as a parent or sibling). A history of abnormal neurological signs or developmental delays prior to the febrile seizure. A febrile seizure lasting longer than 15 minutes. A febrile seizure with strong focal features before, during, or after the event. Management of febrile seizures includes early use of antipyretic medications to reduce fever, which appears to be effective. However, applying cold methods such as tepid sponging is no longer recommended, as it does not provide additional benefits over antipyretic medications. While antipyretic drugs are often advised to reduce fever and potentially lower the risk of febrile seizures following childhood immunizations, there is limited evidence to support their effectiveness in this context. For prolonged seizures (lasting more than 5 minutes), the use of rescue medications, such as benzodiazepines, may be considered. Although some children experience frequent febrile seizures, the routine use of antiepileptic medications to prevent these episodes is generally not justified due to the unfavorable risk-benefit ratio. Certain risk factors increase the likelihood of developing epilepsy after febrile seizures. These include: A family history of epilepsy. Complex features of the febrile seizure. The presence of early-onset neurodevelopmental abnormalities. There is evidence suggesting an association between prolonged febrile seizures and lesions in the temporal lobe, particularly hippocampal sclerosis. However, it is now believed that these brain lesions likely preexist and increase the likelihood of febrile seizures, rather than febrile seizures directly causing temporal lobe epilepsy. The prognosis for febrile seizures is generally favorable. Approximately one-third of children who experience a febrile seizure will have a recurrence. The strongest predictor of recurrence is the age at which the first febrile seizure occurs; the younger the child at the time of the first seizure, the higher the likelihood of recurrence before they outgrow the condition. Most recurrences occur within the first year after the initial episode, and over 90% occur within two years. Other factors that may increase the risk of recurrence include: A family history of febrile seizures (but not epilepsy) in a first-degree relative. An initial seizure occurring with a relatively low fever. Multiple seizures during the same febrile episode. Interestingly, status epilepticus (a prolonged seizure) in an otherwise normal child does not appear to significantly increase the risk of further febrile seizures or the development of epilepsy.
